newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open weaker after dive on Friday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open weaker after dive on Friday.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities opened moderately lower on Monday after a sharp decline late last week.

Analysts said the early weakness was due to minor follow-through selling on the market's decline on Friday after the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) said its diffusion index of industry activity climbed to 58.6 percent in July, its highest since November 1994 when it registered 59.1 percent. The production index read 64.4, a 9-1/2-year high. The new orders item hit a three-year peak.
In early trade on Monday, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 6/32 to 102-3/32, yielding 6.47 percent.
Analysts said a test of 6.50 percent on the 30-year Treasury yield was possible ahead of the Treasury's $38.0 billion refunding effort this week.
The Treasury will sell $16.0 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday, $12.0 billion in 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday.
Separately, the Treasury will sell $17.0 billion in three- and six-month bills on Monday in its weekly bill auction.

After Friday's data onslaught, which besides the key NAPM index, included the monthly U.S. employment report showing unexpectedly strong job growth of 316,000 new jobs in July, the calendar of economic data is light this week.

The only economic report due on Monday is the U.S. construction spending report for June. A Reuters poll culled an average forecast of a 1.1 percent rise in construction spending for June after a 1.8 percent drop in May.
The construction spending report is unlikely to have a big market impact, analysts said.
Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Securities, called the market's early declines "followthrough" from Friday's decline.
"You have the refunding coming up tomorrow and you have a slightly more cautious stance amongst investors following the July employment figures and some of the data in the NAPM," Flanagan said.
Flanagan said the selling represented "a lot of the weaker hands that jumped on the bandwagon" late.
Flanagan said a test of 6.50 percent on the 30-year bond yield would not be surprising.
But he added that for the bond yield to climb above 6.50 percent on a sustained basis, the bond market would need more bad news.
Trading volume was moderate, with GovPX reporting more than $17 billion being exchanged in the first hour of trading.
Analysts said the Fed could add temporary reserves to the banking system through system repurchase agreements on Monday or refrain from operations.

At 0900 EDT/1300 GMT, the two-year Treasury note was down 3/32 to 99-29/32 to yield 5.93 percent. The five-year note was off 7/32 to 99-15/32 to yield 6.13 percent, while the 10-year note was down 11/32 at 102-27/32 to yield 6.23 percent.
The three-, six- and year bill rates were each up one basis point to 5.15 percent, 5.19 percent and 5.23 percent, respectively.
